[unclear] they have never perceived. Just as, if you show to a boy learning the first elements of letters any written volume whose character is unlike that in his own little book, when he cannot read the writing he will at once cry out that it is bad and not properly formed. In the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures, wise only in a fleshly manner, and who do not grasp those things that are of the divine Spirit, burdened by vices and rashness, when they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach as holy the Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not lawful for everyone everywhere to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast, touching the mountain, be overwhelmed with stones.

Many now arise in a reversed order, who have spent the whole time of their life on humane letters; having become older men, they wrongly interpret the divine Scriptures, which they have never learned, and do not explain them but confuse them, examining them according to their own sense. Hence all who do not understand the sacred Scriptures by that Spirit by which they were breathed into those who wrote them have over their hearts the veil of ignorance and rashness, spread out after the manner of the Jews; from there they very often drink the poison of destructive error, from which those who approach humbly in the Spirit of God have received the cup of salvation.

For heavenly doctrine is not contained in the words of the Scriptures, but in their meaning; not on the surface of the words, but in the understanding; not in the leaves of ornate speech, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in the manner of its speech, since in one and the same discourse, while it recounts the text, it reveals a hidden mystery; just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has in public that from which it may nourish little ones; it preserves in secret that by which it may suspend the minds of the lofty in wonder at its sweetness, like a certain marvelous river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim.
Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

And St. Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its strength it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones. For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the perspicacity of human talent. Therefore, in order that one may come to their true understanding, above all the mind must be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the aid of divine goodness must be diligently implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illumine the understanding of the learner.

For all necks of powers must be subjected to the authority of the divine Scriptures. And, as the divine Jerome says, one must never flatter a man in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected; in the whole of both Testaments it is true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terrifyingly to be feared in its threats. Therefore it has not been given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but it is permitted in some measure only to those in whom love makes study continuous, and to whose purified minds the Spirit of God grants true understanding.

But whoever is foul with the darkness of vices, whoever walks with a swollen mind, proud; whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God, whether in part or in whole, let him never trust that he can attain to their understanding. For the authority of Scripture itself says that unless you have believed, you will not understand. The slowness of our talent is ours, and so too the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures, namely when the veil of pernicious occupation
To Maximilian Caesar.

... remains spread over our hearts, which does not permit us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the sense which the Holy Spirit has poured into the divine Scriptures, but, seizing the bare words of the writers, we twist them into another sense. Indeed, if our minds were purged of carnal vices, if through the continual pursuit of sobriety the intellect were stirred up in the Scriptures, if belief and reverence were applied as their dignity requires, every student would understand more clearly than light that in the sacred readings there is nothing confused, nothing misshapen, nothing unsuitable, nothing absurd, or inserted without the most just reason. For all the passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; and whenever anything in them seems to have been set down obscurely, this has been done by divine providence, so that the studious mind may have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple may not lose the place of due reverence. Therefore not by chance, but by eternal providence, he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that it might abound in as many mysteries as senses in which, by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, it is explained in Catholic fashion by the doctors. For, as holy Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it begets many meanings of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; for when one man draws out this sense, and another that sense, while expounding it in Catholic fashion, it becomes known how lofty and deep it is. Therefore let no man swollen with secular learning suppose that he understands sacred Scripture, unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning is of more value for exercising the intellect than for illuminating the understanding toward true wisdom. Therefore without doubt divine Scripture is, to minds purified through the continual exercise of the fear of God and frequent study of reading, both manifest and clear, though to filthy minds, confused by secular wisdom, it seems obscure.
Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection, being frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote. For if they are read in another spirit than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must necessarily be wholly shut away from true understanding. But when we encounter some discordance in them, let us understand that it is only of words, not of meanings; and it arises not by chance but by the ordering providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures, may be strengthened and not become altogether sluggish. For the counsel of God cannot be deceived; but the divine Scriptures were written by the counsel of his will. It follows necessarily that they are true and in no way false. They were men by whom the divine [Scriptures] came to us. You who are devoted to secular wisdom, say of the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, which the Church of Christians has received and venerates as true, authentic, and holy Scripture: whence do you believe it was received, from God or from men? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks the Scripture which he believes to be inspired most openly resists the divine ordering. But if it is from men, why do you hope for the eternal salvation promised in it, which man cannot give? Unless perhaps, madmen, you go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that nothing remains after fate except ashes, and that the mind together with the body undergoes
To Maximilian Caesar

destruction, a profession which would show you to be no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit; but if, having fallen with the apostates into a reprobate sense, you say that they were [composed?] by men, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness, and you openly reveal yourselves to be unskilled and rash judges, since you condemn Scripture which you do not understand. But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind longer against the rashness of emperors. This one thing I want you to know: that no one understands unless he receives; but because you set the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, therefore you do not have the understanding of true wisdom. For almighty God deigns, through grace, to be present as illuminator to those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except for God. The Spirit of God brings help by his presence to those whom he has found rooted in the love of truth, and, having been cleansed from every extraneous thing, he leads them into the knowledge of all things. For to those who truly love God all things are open, all things naked, all things manifest, since whoever, through love, beholds in the faith of Jesus Christ him who creates and governs all things, knows all things that are necessary for his salvation. But, on the contrary, the illumination of God dwells very far from the slothful, the wicked, gluttons, the envious, the avaricious, [incubonibus], the filthy, the lustful, murderers, the impious, the proud, and those alien to piety, leaving them to the discretion of the avenging demon, who, driving in the sharp point of savage fire, afflicts sense and mind, and more and more arms and drives the impious to perpetrate crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also be liable to a sharper punishment.
Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

Whence, entangled in vices and worldly desires, they not only cannot penetrate the divine Scriptures with understanding, but, neglecting themselves, do not even know themselves. Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is the perfect work of God, we must so confirm the mind, Caesar, that we believe it true, right, complete, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith. Indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect, and complete in all things, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Therefore every Christian must take the greatest care that, by scrutinizing the divine Scriptures more than is expedient, he not go beyond the bounds of piety, because the author of the Scriptures is not man, but the Holy Spirit; and whoever resists the integrity of God’s Scriptures is proved to resist his ordinance. Moreover Scripture, by God’s ordaining, is usefully interwoven with parables, enigmas, likenesses, and comparisons of figures, so that readers may be exercised toward understanding and, once the inward sweetness has been tasted, the mind may be confirmed in piety. And so, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of Scripture, not the words, we shall understand how rightly and properly all things have been ordered. For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which the knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so completely full and manifest that they would everywhere be understood by all; what is proposed to be understood is only for the good and holy, not also for evil, filthy, and polluted minds. Hence indeed it is written: “the beast that touches the mountain shall be overwhelmed with stones.” What is designated here by the beast, if not men who, in imitation of brute animals, live without the love of God in pleasures
To Maximilian Caesar.

pleasures of the flesh. And what is expressed by the mountain, if not the height of the divine Scriptures? When a beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a man impure in mind, or weak in regard to the faith, who strives to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a teacher handing it down, is wounded by various and pernicious errors as by blows of stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane. Therefore God placed his hiding-place in the height of the Scriptures, which is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that nevertheless it always lies manifestly open to the saints.

But why almighty God did not give Holy Scripture as sufficient and manifest for all things that concern the Christian faith, we answer briefly. There are two things that the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith, namely the Church and Scripture, so that what is declared in one may be supplied in the other. Hence if we find anything in the Holy Scriptures concerning the rules of faith expressed less sufficiently, we at once have recourse to the Church; and where the Church, in saving instruction, has need of help for piety, it immediately betakes itself to Scripture. Nor would the Church have authority without Scripture, nor Scripture faith without the Church, so that from the two there may be one judgment. For Augustine says: I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me. But Johannes Gersonensis says: I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me. The Church confirms Holy Scripture, and it likewise is confirmed by Scripture. The Church abounds whenever Scripture is lacking. And if at any time the Church is in doubt, it has recourse to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God, who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ, the very same almighty one who alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord, which is not easily broken, where divine Scripture is joined by the Holy Spirit to the authority of the Church to such a degree that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church.

Thus, as it seems to me, O Caesar of unconquered majesty, we have assigned a sufficient reason for the question proposed. For if all things that concern the piety of faith were manifestly expressed in the Holy Scriptures, holy mother Church would not appear to be of such great authority, and the merit of saving obedience would in large part be emptied away. At the same time I think a sufficient answer has been given to the principal question, where certain people suppose Sacred Scripture in very many places to be confused and imperfect; yet if they read it with due purity of mind, they would indeed find it perfect and solid. Great is the authority of the Catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning the faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures; to it the necks of all powers must be subjected. If anyone by rash daring departs from its definition, he has denied the Gospel of Christ. There is one congregation of the faithful, the mother of Christians, the holy Church; outside its unity no one will be saved. And although in morals it may sometimes seem weak, nevertheless in faith it has always remained constant and has never erred, by the preserving mercy of Christ.

On the Reprobate and Witches
Fifth Question

The fifth question of Your Most Serene Highness was this: Why can impious, evil, and reprobate persons in matters of faith, such as those women whom we commonly call witches, command malignant spirits, when good men, and the most zealous observers of the Christian faith, can neither command good spirits nor always malignant ones?

I remember that I formerly answered this question as follows: In all the works of the divine majesty there is an order and sequence of beauty, of immovable equity, by which individual things, suitably disposed, persevere in the rank which they have received. For without its proper order nothing subsists. In the world, in this order, the freedom of will which the Creator gave to all human beings is driven by no violence of power so as not always to remain in the order which the first man received from the beginning of his creation. Hence no one among mortals is good except by the counsel of his own will, assisted by the grace of a merciful God; and no one is evil except of his own accord, deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin. By rectitude of will we are made like good spirits, if we prove the piety of the faith which we have in Christ by holy and necessary works. And just as the consummation of a good will makes good men equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious renders them like demons. Hence evil and perverse people, the more they have been depraved by the malice of their own will,
Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions 48

the more they become like demons in disposition. By likeness, moreover, the familiarity of friendship is introduced, from which mutual confidence is gradually generated. From the confidence of the lesser toward the greater, command arises, whether it is true or feigned by cunning. Therefore, if there seems to be any command of wicked people over demons, it arises from the greatness of their wickedness: namely, when their disposition is depraved to such a degree that, by a reprobate will, they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons joining with them.

For demons are not all equal in malice or intelligence; rather, one is much more cunning than another in quickness of understanding, and far worse in depraved affection. For those who, having fallen from the high seats, dwell nearer the earth and inhabit caverns and caves, are certainly duller than the rest, to such a degree that they fear swords and rods, and seem to be moved by the threats of men who terrify them. This may be observed in those whom we call energumens. But demons who dwell farther removed from the earth are subtler by nature and meet with human beings more rarely. People full of malice, however, the more they advance in perversity of will, the more like demons they become; admitted by them into familiarity, they thereafter become bold, and receive command over the demons whose familiarity they use: a command not of violence, but of pretense. For demons, in order to keep willing in their depravity those people whom they have once received into surrender, gladly subject themselves to them, as though moved by a feigned dominion; what they do voluntarily, they pretend that they are compelled to do in obedience. For no one obtains true command over demons except one whom faith in the Lord [unclear].

... has made our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, acceptable and a friend to God; for thus Scripture says of those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.” Evil men therefore command demons, whom malice has made like to them; likeness made them familiar, and familiarity made them their own and subject.

It is as if some servant, born in a humble station, were said to command a great prince, which often happens, because he has been joined to him by long familiarity; through this he obtains without contradiction everything he has asked, so that he seems rather to rule his lord than to be ruled by him. According to this likeness, evil and reprobate men, who are admitted by demons into their familiarity and become very bold through more prolonged [unclear] confidence, receive a counterfeit, not to say familiar, command over them, which they have deserved by the likeness of a most depraved will. Hence whatever they have sought to receive from demons for themselves by an explicit compact, with [unclear] concurring, they receive, except whenever, being forbidden by divine ordinance, they are unable to furnish what is asked. Yet they do not thus present themselves indiscriminately to all reprobate and evil persons, but only to those with whom, through the intervention of some compact, they have entered into treaties, as are sorcerous women who have done homage to the Devil, and invokers of those same demons, whom the common people call by the customary term necromancers.
There are two kinds of men who may command lawfully.

The first indeed is of those men who, beloved of God by the merit of holiness, have received from him the power of trampling the head of the ancient serpent, such as in the primitive Church were the Apostles and their followers and disciples, concerning whom the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they will cast out demons,” and “they will take up serpents.”

The second kind, however, is of those men to whom, by reason of their order in the Church of God, it is granted that they drive demons out of men’s bodies by the power of the ministry received. And this ministry is entrusted to exorcists in the Church of God, namely when they are ordained by the bishop.
Again there are two kinds of men who desire to command demons; with what unlawful presumption they do this, they show by their most wicked conditions.

The first and most pernicious kind is that of sorceresses, who enter into pacts with demons and, after a solemn profession has first been made, hand themselves over to some demon as property and for perpetual service. How many evils this most pernicious kind of human beings commits in your empire, most wise Caesar, there is no one who can express. For first of all, denying God and the faith of Christ and holy Baptism, they offer themselves, in mind and body, to demons; by their sorcery they make human beings and beasts sick, harm them, and kill them. There is no disease which, if God permits it, they cannot bring on, because, when they present themselves as servants to demons in observance of the compacted treaty, by comparison with them they dare whatever they wish. Hence they are nowhere to be tolerated, but rather in every place are to be utterly exterminated, as God, creator of all, so commands: “You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.” Of sorceresses, some summon demons by spells, others entice them by prayers and sacrifices, the rest by unspeakable things and ceremonies
To Maximilian Caesar 51

Summoning them, they draw them into the assistance of their own impiety. It is therefore not to be wondered at that witches seem to command demons, to whom they have become similar through the impiety of a perverse will, and, by mutual association, are united for the harm of the human race.

The second kind of wicked men who wish to command demons is that of those whom we commonly call necromancers. They profess arts full of execrations, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them openly visible, enclosed in crystal or some other vessel. These most pernicious men, full of falsehood and superstitions, commit evils so great that no good man could think them up.

For, in order to entice demons into service to themselves, they generally use most shameful sacrifices and enter into an express pact with them. They circulate many and various little books, full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, and deceitfully inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and wise men; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious persons, and draw them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise things great and altogether incredible, and by the hearing of these they falsely hold men suspended in wonder.

They say that by rings, pendants, images, exorcisms, and conjurations they can constrain malignant demons so that they appear visibly in a circle or in crystal, or in some vessel, and answer distinctly to all questions asked. All of them indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found to whom malignant spirits, even for evil purposes, are obedient in this way, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it, lest the curiosity of men, prone to novelties, con-

Demons obey, but only those with whom they are allied by pacts and acts of service; and when invoked by those whom they cannot otherwise keep faithful, they gladly come, although they falsely claim that they are compelled. It is therefore no wonder, most excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to obey depraved and perverse men, whom, as we have said, both likeness in malice and the destruction of the human race has made to be in agreement. But far be it from every Christian to wish, through a depraved likeness of will, to command demons. For if anyone in this life has begun to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the future he will burn with them without end.

But why good and righteous men cannot command the holy angels of God, though they have passed into their likeness of good will, I think the solution of this question would easily be given from what has been said above, if the difference of intelligences is recalled to mind. For although in the Church of God there are many men established whose righteousness benefits many unto salvation, yet in our times very few make such progress that, by reason of the merit of holiness, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it comes about that men of our age neither command malignant spirits by merit of holiness nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of holiness by which, working miracles in the Church, they have advanced as the saints once did, then they can both powerfully command demons and have the familiar fellowship of blessed spirits. For it is certain that holy men beloved by God in the primitive Church of the Christians once provided greater benefits to mortals through the cooperation of good spirits than

On the Power of Witches.
Sixth Question

Your invincible Majesty’s sixth question was: whence comes this so great power in witches, by which they are able to perpetrate so many, various, and wondrous things, even in a single hour, of such a kind and magnitude as none of the good could accomplish in his whole life?

If we wish to answer this question briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything. For Christ says in the holy Gospel, “Without me you can do nothing”; hence it is manifest that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God, and from nowhere else, whether men do good or evil. Hence the most holy prelate Augustine says: the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions, and nothing is done visibly in this most ample and immense commonwealth of the whole creation which is not either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments. Hence, Caesar, it must not be doubted that that power of the witches, in which, with the cooperation of demons, they produce wondrous and horrible effects, is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist, and without whose influence a man cannot even move his hand.

For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether to harm a human being or a beast of burden, unless almighty God wills it, consents to it, and grants the power that they may do what they have already resolved upon with perverse will. Unless God consents and wills, no creature can do anything; otherwise, if anything could be done without his willing and consenting, it would necessarily follow that God is weak, since he could not prevent what, against his will, he would be forced to permit to be done. But since every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both willing and being able.

Whatever, therefore, witches do, God permitting it thus, without whose will they could do nothing, since, unless God granted it, they would obtain neither from themselves nor from demons the ability to do what they wish: therefore all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved as in the first cause of all things, since from the one from whom we have received freedom of will, from him also we have the ability to do what we will. But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they perpetrate the evils they do not by human art, but by the cooperation of demons, whom, just as nature has made subtle, so long experience has made swift in producing wonders. For the wondrous effects of witches are not caused by such means as they use for witchcraft, such as heads of the dead, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things similar to these, but by the Devil who instituted these signs; since he is most proud, he desires in all things to be seen as comparable to God. We have ascertained that witches, in times of swollen rivers, have drawn out butter, which can in no way happen otherwise than by the ministry of a demon. In like manner, when they have been brought into hatred of some man or beast and desire his destruction, they are driven by the gravest fury, thinking of nothing in their mind except vengeance. They take things familiar to them, known for witchcraft; they invoke demons; they show the signs instituted by them, together with characters; what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they achieve by the ministry of those demons.

But another person, who is not subjected to demons by a pact of surrender, even if he knows the things suitable for witchcraft and likewise the manner of working, although he displays the signs, rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the familiars of the demons. For the devil is so lifted up with pride that he emulates the Church of Christ: just as one who has not been ordained cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may utter the words of consecration, so also the demon, however much signs or characters are shown to him by one who invokes him, if he does not know that person to be subject to himself by pact, either never or rarely cooperates. For if he came everywhere to all who invoked him, without pacts having been interposed, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership.

Hence it is that many who are given over to profane arts, laboring with dreadful conjurations to summon demons to a circle, to a mirror, or to any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either the command of God stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious man not dedicated to him by homage. For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is clear that none is perpetrated: a witch raging in spirit and depraved in will; also the cooperation of a familiar devil; [unclear].

For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not meet the wicked woman’s will, she would perpetrate no evil deed. Again, if the witch is lacking, the devil will in no way consummate the evil deed. For the devil uses the will of the raving witch, like a craftsman using an instrument for working, without which he cannot inflict the evil deed. And just as demons differ from one another in power and in keenness of subtlety, so the power of witches is not one and the same in all, but is diverse in each individual, according as demons of a subtler or grosser nature concur with them. For there are many kinds of demons, and they are separated from one another by fixed degrees, by reason of the places into which, when they fell at the beginning, they were thrust down.

The first kind of demons is called fiery; it wanders about the upper air and is never cast down to the lower regions before the day of judgment, but, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, has no intercourse on earth with human beings. That it remains beneath the moon, Saint Augustine bears witness in the work On the Christian Combat, saying thus: demons do not dwell in heaven, where the sun and stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region. Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals, because Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals, furnished with little wings, have rather often been seen flying about; they spend their whole life in fire, since they are born with fire and are extinguished with it, and, vanishing, return to the place from which they had come. They have no associations with witches, because, since they dwell in fire, on account of their subtlety they cannot put on a gross or aerial body.

The second kind is called aerial, which, wandering in the air, dwells near us. Indeed they can descend to the lower regions and, having assumed bodies from the thicker air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. With God permitting, they quite often disturb the air, stir up thunder and storms; all together they conspire for the destruction of the human race. They are moved, in the manner of human beings, by the affections of the passions; they are touched especially by pride and envy and by continual disturbances. They are not clothed with a solid body, nor do they remain in one place, nor do they all have one form, but many, and they change these rather often according to the variety of the affections by which, either summoned by the incantations of witches, they come to meet them, or, driven by disturbance, they move to do harm. For they have an altogether violent, frenzied character, full of disturbances; hence, when greatly agitated by evil-working, they very often devise sudden ambushes. While making their attacks, they partly wish to lie hidden, partly they inflict violence. Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are so much the more powerful for evil-working, the higher in that order the one who assists them is whom they have obtained. In the life of Saint Anthony, Saint Athanasius said that the air is full of demons, which Mercury, thrice-greatest, had said before: namely, that no part of the world is devoid of the presence of demons. The third kind, however, we call terrestrial demons, whom we do not at all doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth for their deserts. Concerning these the most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, Theophorus, once Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: “Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and terrestrial spirits alike is made void.” Of these demons, some dwell in woods and groves, and lay snares for hunters. Others live in open fields, and make travelers wander at night; some abide in hidden places and caves; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight to dwell with human beings in darkness. They are not led by one disposition but by a varied one, since some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Of these, some rejoice in terrifying human beings by illusions alone; others desire, by predictions of future events, to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves. Some, however, labor with the greatest effort to this end: that they may terrify, harm, or kill people disturbed by irrational madness or raging with melancholy, which we have recognized by experience to have happened rather often. Hence Saint John Chrysostom, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: “More powerful than every diabolical action for doing no harm is the greatness of sorrow, because the demon overcomes whomever he overcomes through sorrow; if you take this away, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon.” This kind of demons, however, is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy and lightness of its affections, whereby they rejoice in terrifying many rather than in being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet they sometimes dwell with, or make promises to, mad women, in glass or in crystal or in a mirror; and when stirred up by incantations they give replies to women, and if someone who is to come has cursed them on the road, they announce it beforehand. And this kind of witches differs in some respects greatly from the rest, since what the former make sick by witchcraft, these promise to cure. But because for the most part they repel witchcraft by witchcraft, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, since, immersing itself in liquids, it dwells about lakes and rivers, full of anger, disturbed, restless, and deceitful. In the sea it stirs up storms, and, sinking ships into the deep, takes life from many in the waters. And whenever these demons assume a visible body, they more often appear in the female sex, and are more rarely seen in the male, because they live in damp places and follow a softer course of life; nor can they easily assume a base form by the custom of the others. Hence antiquity long ago named the Naiads and Nereids, nymphs of the waters, not in the male but in the female sex. By our people, however, they are called by the common term aquatic women, that is, Wasser Frawen. Those, however, who dwell in drier and rather arid places, whenever they appear bodily visible to human beings, transform themselves into men.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. On Divine Permission
Seventh Question

The seventh question of Your Most Serene Majesty was this: why almighty God, since he is just and the avenger of evils, permits such great misdeeds to be done to the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocent persons perish, grievously tortured.

To this question, when I was formerly placed before your majesty, I remember that I answered as follows. Almighty God, just, upright, kindly, merciful, whatever he permits, permits justly, because he is just; there is no iniquity with him, but in true judgment he either does or permits all things that are done. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, we answer: he permits them because he is just.

Let not the answer we have given seem absurd to Your Majesty, O Caesar, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For indeed, if he did not permit evils to be done, then man could not sin; he would certainly be impeccable, which does not befit his nature, to which from the beginning the creator of all things gave free will. For since man is a creature and not the creator, he is necessarily as capable of being turned to good as to evil; his being depends upon the supreme maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends upon the cause of its being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and eternal; everything corruptible necessarily fails, but it is preserved by the goodness of the creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause. Hence it neither could nor ought to have happened that man, by the condition of his nature, should be created impeccable; naturally this is enjoyed by God alone, the maker of all things, who is immutable and eternal.

But whenever it is granted to man that he seems unable to sin, neither is the freedom of will taken away, nor is the possibility simply removed, but the will is confirmed in good. And whenever this gift is conferred on a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning; he left him in the hand of his own counsel. For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, should have free will and yet be unable to commit sin. For most holy Augustine says: the first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last freedom in glory will be much more [unclear], he would not have dominion over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, he nevertheless justly permits men to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of will remains, the virtue of a good work may receive its merit, and voluntary depravity may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly. Therefore almighty God justly permits men to sin and to do evil, to whom from the beginning he granted freedom of will. But there are many reasons long since assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great crimes to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall briefly make mention in order as necessary.
The first is so that the excellence of the divine power may be manifested, since he alone is immutable above every [unclear].

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, which knows how to draw good from our evils, when it makes one person’s sin become another’s merit, for the increase of virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, which of us would understand the good? For the good of God orders; but evils he does not do, but, when they have been done by the impious, he himself disposes them so that they may not come about in disorder. Nor does the malice of men hinder the will of God, nor can man do anything which God does not permit.

The third cause is that the Almighty permits wicked deeds to be done in order to manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and have done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, neither could God be merciful; but since in many things we all offend, everywhere God finds something to forgive, everywhere a guilty person presents himself, in whom the pious Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy bishop Augustine: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised and would not be sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not be ended. Therefore where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, gathers together into one. Therefore the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason of divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared against those who have sinned and have not done penance, since if all did good and no one sinned, the justice of God would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have a place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will render to each according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse than the beasts, which, with no violence impelling them, freely use the motions of nature. For even if brute animals lack reason, nevertheless they have the free motion of nature, which they follow; in comparison with them man would seem of an inferior condition if he did not have the free choice of the will. But God permitted man a free will, over which neither kings nor princes rule.

The sixth reason is the praise of the merit of constancy in human virtue, since we praise a just man for this reason: that, although he could have transgressed, he did not transgress, but, with the grace of God helping him, remained in the constancy of a good will.

And the first reason is the testing of the faith of Christians and the experience of their integrity: that, scourged by the harmful arts of demons, they may learn, in the sufferings of the flesh, what faith and love toward God they possess in the hidden place of the mind. In prosperity it is not difficult to be long-suffering; but in adversity, to await help from the savior of the faithful with humble patience belongs not to the soft, but to the strong and truly faithful Christians. But he who does not approach sorcerers on these grounds, because God has forbidden it, preferring to live, with observance of God's commandments, in poverty and sickness rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly preserves the integrity of the Christian faith. Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, men corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith are not to be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by harmful arts, who reveal thefts and adulteries by the ministry of demons, who foretell future things by inspection of stones or mirrors. Do not hear them, I pray, who, ignorant of divine law, would wish ministers of demons of this sort to exist under your command, because they know how to undo spells by spells; for such pernicious treatment of bodies brings about the death of souls, and makes men withdraw from God, the creator of all things, and adhere to impious apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

Secondly, the reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be injured by witchcraft is the increase of merits, namely that their patience, proved in tribulation, may deserve a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says: man is unknown to himself, as to what he can bear and what he cannot; sometimes he thought he could not bear what nevertheless he can. When temptation comes, as if some interrogator, a man is found by himself, who before, lying hidden, did not know himself. The divine chief apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others, how inconsiderate and weak he was; he received it, and the weakness that lay hidden appeared. Therefore temptation is the greatest testing of man, as sacred Scripture bears witness,

The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men. Patience is easy in prosperity, when no adversity strikes the mind. But many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the guarding of humility, so that the faithful and righteous man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and with men they shall not be scourged.” Therefore pride held them; they were covered with their iniquity and impiety; their iniquity comes forth as though from fat. It belongs to God’s mercy that he sometimes permits good and righteous men to be shaken by adversities, whom he knows cannot be humbled in prosperity. For tribulation has made many humble whom favorable circumstances would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagining of evildoers makes the good man fear his God and diligently invoke his help, strengthened by which he may trust that he is safe against the assaults of demons. But let no proud man, presuming on his own powers, think himself safe from the harmful arts of demons, since the man whom, swollen with pride, God’s protection abandons, without doubt lies open to the harmful arts of demons.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the witchcrafts of demons to prevail against good and innocent persons is so that an excessively licentious occasion for sinning may be cut off from them. For there are many poor, sick, good, devout, humble persons pleasing to God, whom poverty and bodily illness preserve in the love of God, and who, if they were rich and raised to honors, would quickly fall away from the purpose of holiness into the abyss of vices. It is not beneficial for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health, nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore almighty God, wishing to show his mercy toward those whom he has chosen, permits the good, the just, and the innocent to be subject to various calamities; sometimes through demons, sometimes through evil men, sometimes in diverse other ways and by other means, he takes away from such persons riches and honors, which he foreknew they would use badly, so that they may keep humility in poverty and abasement, which they would certainly not have preserved if placed in wealth and exaltation. He also often permits them to fall into many great illnesses, for whom glad health of the flesh would have brought the greatest sickness of mind.

Finally, he permits certain persons to be driven to death by witchcraft, so that the license for sinning may be cut off from them, which they would have abused had they been allowed to remain longer in life. On the Providence of God. Question Eight.

This was the eighth question of Your Serenity: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as also by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a certain and infallible providence over all and each of those things which are done in the world.

I remember that I answered this question as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence, by whose will and command they were brought forth into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion first, indeed, from the Scriptures, and afterward by arguments, as briefly as may be allowed. In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise King Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth so as to cause your soul to sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest perhaps the Lord, angered against your words, scatter all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies to providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for an as, and one of them does not fall upon the earth before God?” A great commendation of divine providence, which has care not only for men, but also for tiny birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would not believe that he has care for great things? “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” And a little later he adds, saying: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?”

Almighty God, because he created all things and brought them forth into being when they did not exist, rules and governs the universe, lest it slip away and flow into dissolution. This could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is removed, it is necessary that the ordered continuity of the whole universe be thrown into confusion. But the providence of the Creator cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds and gives their food to the beasts of burden, and fills every living creature with blessing, and clothes the grass of the fields, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful comeliness, cannot forget man, whom he created from the beginning in his own image. He cares for all things, who governs all things; and he bears providence not only for man, but also for all beasts of burden, in whose dominion all things are placed, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us now, therefore, consider this immense structure of the whole universe, how in its original arrangement and motion it always persists, ordered in the highest degree, and how that divine and unchangeable providence, unless we stray shamefully in mind, preserves, directs, and governs these things by the clearest reason [unclear].

Therefore the whole of what is anywhere, or can be, is comprehended under the command of one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. To us, however, unexpected events occur, because we are changeable and are changed almost daily, having no determinate knowledge of future things.

But that best maker of all things, God, since he is altogether unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, understands all things together and at once: his providence is not deceived; his will is never varied; his power is not broken; his ordering is not violated; his counsel is never intercepted, even if at times his sentence seems to be changed. Hence, if we attend carefully, we plainly understand that the ends of things and of motions will declare that all these lower things are made, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence; from its command nothing at all is alien.

For God himself, ruler of all things, understands both all things and individual things, not dispersed into many things after our manner, but abiding in himself as one indivisible thing; by gazing upon himself as the exemplar of the whole universe and the cause of causes, and through causes beholding the cause of all things, he cares for all things by beholding them, and provides for individual things, directing them to a good end by an eternal order. Come now, most wise Caesar, so that we may understand divine providence, governing all things, let us use reasons, as briefly as we can, for a more attentive [unclear]. And so, if God's action is his own proper intelligence, which no wise man fails to admit, as at once most eminent and most inward, as much as he acts, just so much does he understand, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but also in the smallest. Therefore he understands individual things. Indeed, from the first Being, through individual things that are beings in whatever way, following in fixed orders, there is the most ample influence; and those things which act after him are everywhere moved and act by his power.
Either, therefore, God understands or acts nothing outside himself, which is false; or, by acting, he also understands all things and individual things.

also understands those same things, which is true. For nothing would ever come to be unless first, to speak in our customary way, it were understood by God himself, who makes these things, just as things are not made by the sun which are not looked upon by it. But because the Almighty understands each and every thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made; from him things have not only that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from him also they have received the proper office of a cause, that is, according to their powers to preserve and care for what they have made. Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, rightly does that first cause naturally have this goodness and providence, so that it cares for all things, each thing that it has made, insofar as it is especially the cause of all and each of them. Indeed, unless these are guarded individually by him who makes them, the common things which are preserved in individuals will never be guarded. For the whole, which consists of parts, will not be preserved if the parts themselves are neglected. Therefore from the intention of the first and greatest common intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things. But it is distinguished of itself from others, and distinguishes the rest among themselves by the rule of its knowledge. Hence, just as God knows each and every thing most distinctly, so he most distinctly rules, moderates, and cares for them. Therefore, most clement Emperor Maximilian, I think it is clear and sufficiently shown that the providence of God, the supreme ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and moderates all lower things, each and every one; otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who watches over them, they would in no way continue this most beautiful order which we perceive. Nor does it escape me how variously the wise men of this world once held opinions about providence.
The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius.

Of these, some thought that this world was made not by providence but by chance. If their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift uncertainly, since the world could perish by the same chance by which it was made.

Against their false opinion others taught that the world could neither have been made without reason, nor certainly stand unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by eternal reason, begetter of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity, and, remaining unmoved, grant that all things be moved.” And again he said: “The generation of all things and the whole progress of mutable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, receive their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.”

Others, however, thought that God cared only for incorruptible things, such as heavenly things, separated substances, and likewise the species of things, but that he did not know all the rest and utterly neglected them. But these men erred shamefully, since the Almighty has providence and care not only for incorruptible universals, but also for corruptible particulars. Hence holy Boethius again says: “Meanwhile the high creator sits, and ruling all things bends the reins: king, lord, source, origin, law, wise arbiter of justice. This is the common love of all things, and they seek to be held by the end of the good, because they cannot otherwise endure, unless, by love turned back again, they flow back to the cause that gave them being.”

Others, however, unable to bear that they themselves would be neglected, exempted man, because of the preeminence of his intellect, from the number of corruptible things, saying that God has care and providence for human beings, but the rest of earthly
To Maximilian Caesar.

to despise all earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has been said, and to bring forward many more things would be wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “Men and beasts you will save, O Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has care equally for all.” Therefore the providence of the divine majesty orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all and each of the lower things, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; its most powerful will produces all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again declares: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.” Therefore let men corrupted in mind, impious and reprobate concerning the Christian faith, blush: men who, puffed up with vain talkativeness, take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the judgment of Firmianus, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he foresees nothing, if he neglects lower things, if he does not care for mortal things, he has already lost all dignity. But it is impossible, as holy Anselm attests, for God to lose his honor, since, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, nor corruption, nor sin. Therefore he who removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say except that God does not exist?

But now let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things tell me. If God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is thereafter no reason why we should pursue him with worship or venerate him with religious devotion as a benefactor; indeed rather, being neglected and despised, let us ourselves neglect him too. But if, not knowing, he despises and neglects us, there is now utterly no reason why we should worship one who does not know us and for that reason is unable to confer any good, or invoke him with prayers.
Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

For if God does not care for human affairs, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause of piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope of the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human affairs? Indeed, if providence is removed, whom do we worship, whom do we adore? If there is no providence for mortals with God, certainly he neither bestows benefits on human beings nor imposes punishments on deserters, nor can or will he help mortals, nor does he care at all, nor notice what we do, and he hears neither the entreaties nor the prayers of anyone. But why do we offer him any worship, why honor, why prayers, or why do we so greatly fear or dread a God who does not know us, who, with us neglected and despised, can do us neither good nor ill? For with providence removed, neither holiness nor religion will remain; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and a dreadful confusion will follow. With piety toward God removed, what will the commonwealth then be, except everlasting confusion? Public trust among human beings will necessarily perish, and the fellowship of the human race, and all justice will vanish and perish at once. What is to be thought of the Christian faith, if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, of the Savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, except that the whole will be regarded as an empty fable and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Surely whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us, if he has no care for us at all.
Let those now see and shudder who [unclear] the providence of God

[unclear] of God, when they behold as the end of their opinion the worst despair of all. Therefore let no one, led by the vain talk of secular philosophers, train himself to contempt of God; let no one take away the providence of the supreme and unchangeable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of, and ungrateful for, the benefits of the most merciful Savior.

For it must be firmly believed, and in no way doubted, that this whole world, both visible and invisible, and all and each of the things that are either in heaven or on earth and in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is foreign to his care. For the crops and all the other things that the earth brings forth, and also the storms and the variations of times and the changes of the sky, by which all things that the earth naturally produces grow to maturity, divine providence supplies to the human race; and it provides for all things and each thing, not only the great, but even the very least, to such a degree that not even the slightest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created it and rules and cares for it. But if anyone thinks that this so great magnitude of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by the one God, who alone exists, he is greatly deceived, and is shown not to know how great is the power of divine might. For indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being can also govern forever, most wisely, what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, can do all things, who alone, omnipotent, created all things.

We therefore, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence, and should also lift up our minds, with whatever strength we can, from those things that are perishable; and, brought back to ourselves, we should be united, so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God, present everywhere. Since it is altogether uncircumscribable, it holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. Yet it does not sustain on one side and surpass on another, nor fill on one side and encompass on another; rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining it surpasses, and by surpassing it sustains all things. He is nowhere through the bulk of a body, nowhere absent through his uncircumscribable substance; he is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but is seen through faith in purity of heart. O inexplicable power, O incomprehensible loving-kindness, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity, which does not consist of parts like a body, is not separated by affections like a soul, does not underlie forms like all other things that were made through you, who are in all things, above all things, ruling and governing the universe most wisely.

By these testimonies, therefore, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, it has been sufficiently proved, as I think, that this whole world is governed by the providence of God. Since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and everlasting, he knows all things, understands all things, foreknows all things; and since he is of an omnipotent nature, being all-powerful, he can do all things. Nothing is difficult for him, nothing impossible; he created such wondrous things by his power, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by virtue, illumines them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, God glorious and exalted, forever and ever. Amen.

These are the things, most unconquered Caesar Maximilian, that seemed to me necessary to say in response to the eight questions proposed by your majesty. For you wished to have my judgment too, in writing, concerning them, making an estimate of me beyond the truth; for I am not to be compared in talent with those whose opinion you heard before me. Let pardon make me worthy, if I have said anything less appropriate, because, a traveler set upon the road, at the command of your loftiness, I dictated, as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me that should be answered. But I say from my heart and openly declare that I, a sincere confessor of the Christian faith, wish to remain in union with the most holy Roman Church until death. Therefore, if anything should be held to have been said or written, either in these or in other matters, otherwise than that Church holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, as a true son of obedience I declare by the attestation of the present writing, and I simply wish it to be

to be and to be regarded as forever revoked. Therefore, most wise Caesar, I humbly ask and urgently admonish your Majesty that, before you cause my replies to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined and kept, you have them approved by the judgment of many. For the greatest care must be taken that nothing be set before those for whose salvation your Serenity keeps watch, unless it is sound, tested, clear, and lawfully confirmed by the opinion of very many wise men in the Catholic faith. May almighty God by his providence direct and preserve you always, to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neumarkt, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the Christian year one thousand five hundred and eight.
